meta: AI has billions of knobs, and the mistake only shows up at the end. How does it know which knob to fix? Like a kitchen whose soup is too salty: the head chef traces back each step. That's backpropagation.
prompt: Paragraph 2 has the wrong numbers. Please fix that paragraph.

muc.title: Which knob caused the mistake?
muc.text: Last time: AI walks downhill in small steps to reduce the error. But with billions of knobs, how does it know which ones to turn, and by how much?

muc.title: A bowl of noodle soup sent back
muc.text: Picture a noodle soup kitchen with three cooks: one makes the broth, one cooks the noodles, one does the seasoning. A customer complains: the soup is too salty.

muc.title: Trace back through each step
muc.text: The head chef doesn't scold the whole kitchen. He traces back from the bowl to each step. The heavy-handed seasoner has to change a lot, the noodle cook barely changes at all.

muc.title: The mistake flows backward
muc.text: A neural network does exactly that. The mistake at the output is passed back through each layer, from the last layer to the first. This is called backpropagation.

muc.title: More blame, bigger fix
muc.text: Connections that caused more of the mistake get turned more, those that caused less get turned less. In a single backward pass, the machine knows how to fix every knob at once.

muc.title: The foundation of AI
muc.text: Backpropagation plus gradient descent is the foundation of modern AI. The chatbots you use today were all trained this way.

muc.title: Point to the exact mistake
muc.text: When AI gets something wrong, don't just say "that's wrong". Point to the spot: "paragraph 2 has the wrong numbers, fix that paragraph". AI doesn't relearn during a chat, but pointing to the mistake helps it fix the right thing.

muc.title: What about a new kind of test?
muc.text: Learning this way, a machine can get so good it memorizes all the practice questions. But what happens with a question it's never seen? See you in part 5.
